strengths: Timely and well-motivated problem: the paper convincingly demonstrates that offline SFT performance is a misleading proxy for post-RL performance, with concrete rank reversals across objectives (Fig. 1, Tables 6-7). This is a useful and practically important observation for the SFT→RL pipeline.

The proposed PEAR reweighting is simple, principled in spirit (OPE/importance-sampling), and a genuine plug-in: it augments standard NLL and KL-based distillation with little overhead (Fig. 4b), which lowers the barrier to adoption.

Broad empirical scope: six base models of varying sizes/families (Qwen3 0.6B/1.7B/4B/8B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Math, DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-1.5B), two task families (synthetic logic games and math reasoning), plus a transfer experiment to a shifted RL task distribution (Table 4).

The mechanistic analysis (gradient rotation between offline and online updates, Fig. 7; parameter drift via NSS, Fig. 8) provides suggestive insight into why a better RL initialization differs from a better offline checkpoint, beyond raw accuracy numbers.
The negative-example repulsive variant and the block-level variant show sensible engineering for variance control in long-horizon importance weighting.
weaknesses: No variance estimates, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds are reported anywhere, despite central claims resting on RL training (GRPO) plus stochastic pass@k evaluation. The logic-game numbers in Table 6/7 are quantized to 1.25% increments (suggesting very small evaluation sets), so small deltas (e.g., +1, +2) cannot be distinguished from noise. This is a serious reproducibility and soundness gap.

The central methodological framing is conceptually loose: the 'target policy' in the importance ratio π_θ/π_β is the model being trained, so it is a moving, self-referential target. The change-of-measure justifications in Appendix B/C assume a fixed target policy, and stop-gradient on the weights does not resolve the fact that the target changes every step. The paper does not discuss this, and it is unclear what objective is actually being optimized.

Key hyperparameters (per-decision clip range [-0.08, 0.3], discount γ, block size B, negative weight λ, and the clip bounds G_min/G_max) are either not reported or not ablated. The very narrow, asymmetric log-ratio clip in particular looks heuristic and may dominate the method's behavior, but no sensitivity analysis is provided.

Missing direct comparisons to the concurrent SFT-reweighting methods the paper cites (iw-SFT, DFT, Proximal-SFT, OPC-SFT, A-SFT). The 'single-step IS' baseline is a self-implementation, and the claim that single-step weighting is 'less effective' rests on that single reimplementation.

Presentation and internal consistency are poor: the method is variously called PEAR, PEAR_{B=1}, 'Ours_token', and 'IS-SFT' across figures/tables, making results hard to track; several references point to the wrong exhibit (e.g., 'Figure 4a As shown in Table 4', 'Figure 4b show that...'); Table 1 duplicates an 'SFT+KL' row; Appendix D is empty; and there are typos ('by by 40%', 'hPEAR', 'modle').

Some reported gains are implausibly large and inconsistent (e.g., DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-1.5B +50 on AIME24 pass@64 and +36 on AIME25, while Qwen3-8B shows 0 gain on AIME25 pass@8/64). Combined with the absence of variance, these invite skepticism about whether the deltas reflect the method rather than run-to-run variance or evaluation-set size.

The headline claim of '40% absolute accuracy' improvement on logic games in the abstract/introduction is not clearly traceable to a specific, controlled comparison, and the offline-vs-online advantage of PEAR is partly an artifact of SFT initializations that are unusually weak offline (e.g., SFT 6.2% in Fig. 4a), which deserves more careful normalization.

The OPE theoretical scaffolding is decorative: the practical algorithm uses clipping and discounting that break the unbiasedness the derivation relies on, so the theory does not actually support the estimator as used.

strengths: The central observation—that offline SFT performance is an unreliable proxy for post-RL performance, with documented rank reversals across ~19 objectives (Fig. 1, Tables 6–7)—is a genuinely useful and well-motivated empirical finding that complements and extends Kang et al. (2025). The controlled, contamination-free SynLogic setup and the systematic sweep over probability-based objectives make this part of the story credible.

The proposed PEAR reweighting is simple and plausible, and the three variants (sequence-, token-, block-level) are clearly described with pseudocode (Algorithm 1). The intuition figure (Fig. 2/3) communicates the behavior-target mismatch well.

The empirical evaluation is broad: 6 model families/sizes (Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B, DS-Qwen-1.5B, Qwen3-0.6/1.7/4/8B), two task families (logic games, math), multiple benchmarks, and both NLL- and KL-based offline objectives. Reported post-RL gains are consistent in sign across most settings (Table 2), and the single-step-IS ablation (Table 3) supports the claim that suffix-level credit matters.

The analysis section (gradient principal-angle alignment with GRPO, parameter-drift/NSS measurements in Fig. 7–8) offers a nontrivial mechanistic story for why PEAR helps, which is more than most reweighting papers attempt.
weaknesses: The theoretical framing substantially overstates the rigor of the method. The paper invokes OPE change-of-measure to justify importance weights w = prod_t pi_theta/pi_beta, but the actual algorithm clips per-token log-ratios to the very tight range [-0.08, 0.3] (i.e., ratios in ~[0.92, 1.35]) and clips the aggregated weight to [-10, 5] in log space, with a discount gamma. The resulting estimator is heavily biased and no longer the unbiased IS estimator the theory claims; the paper never analyzes or even acknowledges this bias-variance trade-off, so the OPE justification is largely decorative.

It is unclear when the target-policy probabilities pi_theta are evaluated. The abstract claims 'little additional training overhead once probabilities for the offline data are collected,' but pi_theta changes every step, so weights must be recomputed each step. If weights are instead computed once from the initial checkpoint, the method is quite different and the claim is misleading. This ambiguity directly affects reproducibility.

Several key hyperparameters are arbitrary and unjustified: clip range [-0.08, 0.3], gamma = 0.999 (for sequences of thousands of tokens this aggressively down-weights earlier positions, e.g., 0.999^2000 ~ 0.14), and the weight clip bounds. No sensitivity analysis is provided, and the tight per-token clip plausibly makes PEAR close to uniform weighting, which would undermine the claimed mechanism.

The paper's novelty relative to concurrent work is not clearly established. The related-work section itself lists iw-SFT, DFT, A-SFT, Proximal-SFT, and OPC-SFT, all of which reweight SFT by probability/trust-region ratios. The 'single-step IS' baseline is essentially the generic form of those methods. The only claimed distinction—that PEAR targets RL readiness rather than stabilization—is asserted rather than demonstrated (e.g., no head-to-head against iw-SFT/DFT under identical pipelines).

The presentation is poor and in places broken. There are garbled/duplicated sentences ('Figure 4a As shown in Table 4', 'good SFT...', the KL paragraph in the introduction cut mid-sentence), inconsistent figure references, and figure captions that do not match their content. Table 3 and Table 4 report incompatible numbers for what appears to be the same PEAR+GRPO condition (e.g., 1.7B: 29% vs 38.3%; 4B: 49% vs 59.8%), and Table 3's row/column structure is not self-consistent with its caption.

Some results undercut the strength of the claims. In Table 2, the 8B model shows 0 gain on AIME25 pass@8 (35% vs 35%) and pass@64 (53% vs 53%), and the DS-Qwen-1.5B column shows implausibly large deltas (+50, +36) relative to all other models, suggesting the gains are highly heterogeneous and possibly model/scale-specific. The large DS-Qwen deltas are not explained.

The interpretation of the post-RL comparison is confounded by design: PEAR checkpoints are often weaker offline than SFT (the paper acknowledges this), so a fair question is whether RL simply benefits from a lower, less-committed initialization rather than from genuine mismatch correction. The paper does not control for this (e.g., by matching offline accuracy or by reporting RL gains as a function of offline strength).

Reproducibility of the RL stage is limited: GRPO hyperparameters are stated in one line (lr 1e-6, batch 128, KL 0.01) with no seed/variance reporting, and the offline data construction ('~100,000 correct trajectories', 50K negatives) is only loosely specified. No variance or confidence intervals are reported for the headline claims.

strengths: Addresses an important and practically relevant question: whether offline SFT performance is a reliable proxy for post-RL performance. The paper convincingly demonstrates rank reversals and non-monotonic behavior (Fig. 1, Tables 6-7), which is a genuinely useful empirical finding for the post-training community.

The method (PEAR) is principled rather than ad hoc: it is grounded in off-policy evaluation / importance sampling, with a clear change-of-measure derivation (Appendices B and C) that explains why suffix/continuation ratios are the right object to reweight.

Extensive, well-controlled experiments: 6 base models of varying sizes/families, two task families (synthetic logic games and math reasoning), multiple benchmarks (AIME24/25, AMC23, Olympiad, MATH500), and three PEAR variants (sequence, token, block) plus a negative-example variant.
Consistent post-RL gains over strong baselines (Tables 2, 3, 4), including plug-in compatibility with KL-based knowledge distillation and transfer to a different online RL task distribution.

The analysis (gradient principal-angle alignment with GRPO, parameter drift via NSS, KL/sparsity metrics) provides a mechanistic story for why PEAR-initialized checkpoints require less correction during RL, going beyond a single headline number.
weaknesses: Presentation contains multiple errors that hamper clarity: PEAR_{B=1} is described as 'token-level weighting (§3.3)' while §3.3 is sequence-level and §3.4 is token-level; typos ('by by', 'hPEAR', 'modle', 'netrics'); Figure 1's caption reference to '19 Models' is unexplained; and the abstract's '14.6% pass@8 gain on AIME-2025' vs. the introduction's '40% absolute accuracy' claim do not cleanly match the reported tables.

Result heterogeneity is large and unexplained. DeepSeek-Distill-Qwen-1.5B shows enormous gains (e.g., +36/+50 pass@64 on AIME24), while Qwen3-8B shows ~0 improvement on several AIME metrics. The paper does not analyze when/why PEAR helps most, which weakens the generality of the central claim.

No explicit limitations section and only a minimal impact statement. Given the strong claims, a candid discussion of failure modes (e.g., when the behavior policy is very far from the target, or when offline data is not from a single identifiable behavior policy) is warranted.

The relationship to concurrent importance-weighted SFT methods (iw-SFT, DFT, A-SFT, Proximal-SFT, OPC-SFT) is argued conceptually (stabilization vs. RL-readiness) but never empirically compared, so the claimed advantage over these close relatives is not directly established.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed: no mention of released code, and some baseline hyperparameters (TALR, Beyond-Log-Likelihood objectives) are referenced to prior work rather than fully reported. The discount factor is set to γ=0.999, effectively removing discounting, yet the variance/credit-assignment motivation for it is not ablated.

The '40% absolute' and related headline claims appear to come from a single favorable SynLogic configuration; the more modest, more representative gains elsewhere should be foregrounded to avoid overstating the contribution.
